Jim Barne and Kit Buchan’s songs and dialogue are snappy and cute enough to overcome the overly familiar story arcs.

Braun, who acquits himself well, may be a stage novice, but he’s smart enough to know that the way to raise his game is by going toe-to-toe with one of the best in the business: back-to-back Tony winner (Purpose, Purlie Victorious) and consecutive four-year nominee Kara Young.
Gruesome Playground Injuries is anchored by the well-matched performances of Nicholas Braun and Kara Young, as vulnerable as open wounds.

Without question, both Young and “Succession” star Nicholas Braun, in a stunning New York theater debut, make a much more persuasive case for the play than the show’s production at Second Stage did back in 2010.
Young delivers the best performance by an adult actor of a child character since Anika Noni Rose played a kid in the original 2003 production of 'Caroline, or Change.'
But what the play adds up to eludes me.
While 90 minutes may sound short, Gruesome Playground Injuries ends up undercooked and overlong.
Gruesome Playground Injuries is a warm, inviting play bereft of sentimentality and strong on relationship.
In the reliable hands of veteran director Neil Pepe, it's a slice-of-life one-act with the emphasis on slice.

Gruesome Playground Injuries is a compelling, rigorously performed response to the world, a play that understands how intimacy is often born from shared pain, even when the reasons we cling to it remain elusive.
Gruesome Playground Injuries mostly succeeds as an acting exercise, where the performers can throw themselves (sometimes literally) into showy recklessness.

cn.t: Joseph's macabre two-hander about damaged souls earns mixed reviews, with critics praising Young and Braun's chemistry and performances but finding the play's quirky pain-as-connection premise more clever than emotionally resonant.

vr.q: I had high hopes for Gruesome Playground Injuries but it was a little underwhelming.
